name: Presto (PrestoDB)
summary: Facebook’s distributed SQL engine, now governed by the Linux Foundation, moving its workers from Java to C++ on Velox. Trino is its 2019 fork.
intro: A Presto cluster has a Java coordinator, which parses, plans and schedules each query, and many workers that read data through connectors and pass intermediate results to each other in memory, stage to stage. Connectors cover Hive Metastore tables, Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi, Kafka, MySQL, PostgreSQL and many more, so one query can join a lake table with a live database. Workers come in two kinds. Java workers support every connector and function. Presto C++ workers, developed as Prestissimo, are a drop-in replacement built on Meta’s Velox library: they speak the same REST protocol to the coordinator, need no JVM, and cover the Hive connector (reads and writes), Iceberg (reads only), TPC-H, TPC-DS and JMX. For jobs too big for one cluster’s memory, Presto on Spark runs the same plans as Spark jobs.

Presto is free under Apache 2.0 and governed by the Presto Foundation under the Linux Foundation, whose founding members were Facebook, Alibaba, Twitter and Uber. Releases keep the `0.x` numbering: 0.299 came out in August 2026, and the Java processes require Java 17. IBM, which bought the Presto startup Ahana in 2023, sells Presto as an engine in watsonx.data; Amazon EMR offers both PrestoDB and Trino. Amazon Athena started on Presto in 2016, but its engine version 3 is built from Trino.
strengths: Interactive SQL across many sources: lake tables in the Hive Metastore or Iceberg, plus operational databases, in one query
C++ workers on Velox are a drop-in replacement for JVM workers, with the same coordinator and clients
Presto on Spark runs the same SQL on Spark for very large batch jobs, using Spark’s resource isolation and materialized exchange
Neutral governance under the Linux Foundation, with Meta, Uber and IBM among the companies running and developing it
limits: Easy to confuse with Trino: they share a history, but have developed separately since 2019 (different workers, Java versions, fault tolerance and release numbers), and the creators who named Presto now lead Trino
C++ workers are still in active development: only a few connectors, Iceberg read-only, no custom plugins or user-supplied functions, and some types and functions missing
For the very largest jobs Presto’s answer is a second system: Presto on Spark needs a Spark cluster plus its own package and launcher
Managed offerings lag upstream: Amazon EMR 7.14 ships Presto 0.287 while the project is at 0.299

sections.title: Presto or Trino today?
sections.intro: Both descend from the code Facebook open-sourced in 2013. After the 2019 split they kept similar architectures (a coordinator, workers and connectors) but went separate ways on how workers run and how big jobs survive failures.

story: In 2012 Facebook’s warehouse held more than 300 petabytes in Hadoop, and analysts queried it through Hive, whose MapReduce jobs were built for throughput, not quick answers. Martin Traverso, Dain Sundstrom, David Phillips and Eric Hwang started Presto that fall as an interactive engine that streams data between stages in memory. It went into production in early 2013 and was open-sourced that November.

In 2018 Facebook wanted tighter control over the project, and the creators left to continue their version as PrestoSQL. In September 2019 Facebook, Alibaba, Twitter and Uber formed the Presto Foundation under the Linux Foundation, which also took the Presto trademark, and in December 2020 PrestoSQL was renamed Trino.

Meta kept investing in Presto: hierarchical caching, Presto on Spark for jobs that need hundreds of terabytes of memory, and Velox, a C++ execution library published in 2022 that became the basis of Presto’s native workers. IBM joined through its 2023 acquisition of Ahana.

choices.why: Hive’s MapReduce jobs wrote every stage to disk. Streaming data between stages as it is produced made ad-hoc queries interactive.

choices.choice: Connectors instead of its own storage
choices.why: Facebook’s data lived in several systems. A storage plug-in API let one engine query all of them, which is why Presto can join Hive tables with MySQL.

choices.choice: Run on Spark for the biggest jobs
choices.why: Interactive clusters with small memory headroom could not finish huge ETL queries reliably. Presto on Spark keeps Presto’s SQL and planner but borrows Spark’s resource management and materialized shuffles.

choices.choice: Move execution to a shared C++ library
choices.why: Meta had many engines with separate, hard-to-maintain executors. Velox gives Presto, Spark and other systems one vectorized engine, and lets workers drop the JVM.

timeline.text: Presto started at Facebook in the fall
In production early in the year; open-sourced in November
Presto Foundation forms under the Linux Foundation in September
The creators’ fork, PrestoSQL, is renamed Trino in December
Meta publishes Velox, the C++ library behind Presto’s native workers
IBM acquires Ahana and joins the Presto Foundation
